Perhaps, but there's nothing to lead one to this conclusion. Some cards one
sees abused and can tell, "that can't be what the designer had in mind."
Siren's Lure as written doesn't really give that impression, at least not
obviously so.

> - consistency with other rulings on a related topic
>

The rulings for Illusions of the Kindred/Psyche! as well as Form of Mist and
Psyche! do not bear much relation to this ruling. The absence of this
ruling would not be inconsistent with the existence of those rulings.

> - needless complexity with an alternative ruling
>

Limiting the number of pending combats to no more than 2 is not as simple as
not limiting the number of pending combats. To avoid needless complexity,
it is generally advisable, when possible, to limit a value or event to 0, 1,
or an infinite number (i.e. no limit).

> - extremely tricky timing issues

I haven't heard any mentioned.

> - overall design considerations, perhaps regarding future sets

Impossible to know.

> - balance considerations, regarding the inherent ability of a
> clan/discipline to afford block cancellation
>

This is the only one that makes sense in the current context. Your other
answers, at least the ones that *might* be true, are things that you can't
know, and thus if those were the reasons, a question of why would be
warranted. You have a point here, in that having enough Daughters can
essentially make any action unblockable. However, this costs an untapped
minion (who may get beat down in combat) and a card for each potential
blocker. I hardly ever see decks anymore that leave more than 1 minion
untapped to block, and the fixed Wake makes it hard to have more than 2 or
at most 3 in a turn, much less in a single action. Therefore, you would
get essentially the same effect from Seduction + either Call of the Hungry
Dead or Elder Impersonation, without needing extra modifying vampires and
without worrying that your poor fragile Daughter will get pounded into snot
(and even in this era of widespread toolboxing, I still maintain that you
have no business blocking unless you're building your deck around it, which
means that you fully intend to make that little wench pay for her
insolence).

On the other hand, a 0 blood cost card that cancels a block is pretty strong
even without being stackable (yay power rare!), so it's debatable, and I'd
be willing to accept for the sake of argument that it's broken as written.
If the card has been errata'd for balance reasons, then fine. But why the
harsh reaction to the question? I mean, sure, there *could* be numerous
reasons, but I believe the question was about the particular reason that
instigated the ruling.

In message <aFB48.71$Kc7.476@rwcrnsc54>, Chris Berger

<ark...@ugcs.caltech.edu> writes:
>> Bum's Rush doesn't generate a "combat for later" effect.
>> It causes combat. No pending.
>>
>As soon as the action resolves, there is one combat about to happen.

No, there is one combat happening - but only when the action resolves.

> You
>can play "about to enter combat cards" etc. With Siren's Lure, you would
>then have 2 pending combats in the "queue".

Bum's Rush does not queue a combat. It happens, setting up an entering
combat phase for the purposes of cards which work there, as is the case
with all entering combat effects.

Siren's Lure, however, takes effect when it resolves, but the combat
doesn't. Bum's Rush takes effect when it resolves, as does the combat.

The former is an example of queueing.

Umm... well, yeah, I can sort of see why one would think that queueing up
multiple combats could lead to complex timing issues, but I have yet to see
any arise. On the other hand, the primary effect of Siren's Lure is to
queue up one combat after another (assuming block combat or rush combat is
the result of the action). The primary effect of Siren's Lure is sort of
confusing and introduces the queueing (I can't figure out if that's the
right way to spell that...) of combats as a new mechanic. However, the
playing of multiples of them doesn't really bring up any issues or mechanics
that are not already covered by the card's existence in the first place
(except which combat resolves first, but solving that problem doesn't
require the current ruling by any means). The thing about a queue is... you
can't have a queue with just one thing in it... that's not a queue of
combats, that's one combat. Once you start adding combats to the queue, you
have no added complexity by allowing the queue to grow.

I guess I'll follow the same drill as in the past and just pretend that the
ruling is actually errata, made for balance reasons, which I would find to
be at least semi-reasonable, if debatable.

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On Fri, 25 Jan 2002 17:52:51 -0500, LSJ wrote:

>Queuing multiple combats is a needless complication.

Many other CCG seem to have no problem with this, from the grandaddy
of them all, Magic, to a recent example like the LotR CCG. All you
need is a procedure for ordering them - LIFO, FIFO or phasing player
chooses.

>See also the ruling that Psyche! disrupts Form of Mist.

If you extend that into a general principle then it would follow that
a second Siren's Lure could be played but that its pending combat
would replace the one waiting from the first Siren's Lure. And if the
original acting minion went on to have combat with a third blocker and
one of them used something like Psyche to create yet another pending
combat then that would wipe out the combat waiting from the second
Siren's Lure too.

That seems a weird way of doing things - just having combats evaporate
because the game's memory can't hold them. I suppose that you're
afraid of dealing with timing rules and want to keep the game as
simple as Pokemon. That may be a reasonable idea but you shouldn't
then create cards like Siren's Lure which obviously imply the
possibility of an indefinite number of pending combats.

Andrew

Siren's Lure is hardly the thing causing the confusion here. Although,
there's actually not that much confusion, really. The Form of Mist and the
Blissful Agony have both essentially been lost, by prior ruling. The
Illusions of the Kindred ends combat, and starts a new one with the vampire
from your crypt. Once that combat is finished, the action and resulting
block combat are completely finished, so the first Siren's Lure kicks in,
followed by the second.

There are only two things confusing here. a) Is the combat from Illusions
of the Kindred cancelled because there is a Siren's Lure pending? Normally,
this would not be at all confusing. The answer would be no. I'm unsure,
however, whether the new ruling about queueing multiple combats applies
here, as I still don't really understand what allows a combat to be added to
the queue and what doesn't. Is it illegal to play a Psyche! when combat
ends if there is a Siren's Lure combat pending? So the first confusing
point is brought about *because* of the new ruling, not because of its
absence. b) What order do the Siren's Lure combats resolve in. All that's
needed here is a ruling that says either 1) The acting methuselah orders the
combats as he wishes, or 2) The combats occur in the order that the Siren's
Lures were played.

Granted, the current ruling does away with the need for ruling what order
Siren's Lure combats happen in, but that doesn't mean that it makes your
situation above any clearer.

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson

On 27 Jan 2002 01:03:16 GMT, Halcyan 2 wrote:

>Minion A attempts a Bum's Rush on Minion Z.
>
>Minion Y attempts to block but Minion B plays Siren's Lure.
>
>Minion X attempts to block but Minion C plays Siren's Lure (assuming we have it
>the way *some* people want it, with multiple queuing).
>
>Minion W successfully blocks Minion A. During combat, Minion A plays Form of
>Mist to continue the action.
>
>Minion W plays Psyche!, and another combat starts. Minion A plays Blissful
>Agony but Minion W continues with Telepathic Tracking. Next round, Minion W
>plays Illusions of the Kindred.
>
>So...for all of you queuing fans, exactly what should be happening *now*???

What ought to happen is:

1. Minion A fights the illusory vampire conjured by IotK

2. Minion X fights Minion C and Minion Y fights Minion B (the pending
Siren's Lures). These are simultaneous and so the phasing player can
decide which to do first. Do one and then the other.

The Blissful Agony and Form of Mist/Bum's Rush should both fizzle
because their combat ends effect was cancelled by Psyche! and
Telepathic Tracking (as per the original Wylie ruling).

My test case would be to suppose that you block someone who diverts
the blocker with Siren's Lure. You then deflect the action elsewhere;
the new target then blocks and plays Blissful Agony to end the
resulting combat. Does he get told that he can't play this card
because someone else has already grabbed the "pending combat" slot?
That would be wrong because the Blissful Agony combat follows straight
on while the Siren's Lure combat waits until the action is resolved -
it's not the same timing slot.

It's only Siren's Lure that gives you a separate pending combat later
on - the other cases just replace one combat with another which is
supposed to take place immediately. Resolving multiple Siren's Lures
isn't rocket science - just let the phasing player decide in which
order to take them.

Another case where you get forking is two simultaneous Blissful
Agonies. This can be handled in a similar way and takes place earlier
than any pending Siren's Lures. I see no need to discard the effect
of either card - the combatants each go off to fight a new opponent -
what's the problem? It might get complex if everyone's using Blissful
Agony but hard cases make bad law - in practise this isn't going to
happen.

Still "too confusing"? One hears of primitive tribes that only live
in the present and can't count past three but one would have thought
that VTES players were more advanced. What might be confusing is use
of the word "queue". I thought Americans weren't familiar with this
word - that's why they "stand in line" instead. But their lines can
certainly have more than one person in them, especially at conventions
like Gencon and Origins!

Andrew

--------------------------------------------------------

FYI here are relevant card texts which I looked up in the course of
this.

Blissful Agony
Strike: combat ends. Choose a minion controlled by another Methuselah
other than the opposing vampire's controller. The opposing vampire
enters combat with that minion.

Bum's Rush
Do not replace until the end of this action.
(D) Enter combat with a ready minion controlled by another
Methuselah. The acting minion gets an optional maneuver during
this combat.

Psyche!
Only usable at the end of a combat when both combatants
are still ready. Combat starts again. This is considered an entirely
new combat: weapons can contribute their maneuvers for a second time,
and so forth.

Form of Mist
Strike: combat ends. When played by an acting vampire,
this card counts as an action modifier and the action continues
at +1 stealth as if unblocked (this action can still be blocked).

Siren's Lure
[mel] Only usable by an untapped ready vampire other than the
acting minion when a minion attempts to block. That minion cannot
block this action. Tap this vampire and that minion. Once the
action resolves, this vampire enters combat with that minion.
[MEL] As [mel] above, but do not tap this modifying vampire.

Telepathic Tracking
Only usable when both combatants are still ready and combat
is about to end (with no uncanceled press to continue). Combat
does not end; another round starts.

Illusions of the Kindred
Only usable before range is determined.
Combat ends. Move the bottom card of your crypt to your ready
region. He or she does not contest any other vampires or titles in
play. The vampire has an amount of blood equal to half of his or her
capacity (round down). Combat begins between the vampire and the
opposing minion. Remove the vampire from the game at the end of
combat.

that another might have trouble singing a different song at the same
time too. But the card should be considered innocent until proven
guilty - I can't see it giving much trouble in practise.

On Tue, 29 Jan 2002 08:02:17 -0500, LSJ wrote:

>Incindentally, please learn how to cite messages you look up,
>so that the source can be verified.

If you want to verify a quote then cut and paste it into a search
engine like Google. This takes you straight there. But you needn't
worry - I don't make things up. That's your job <grin>.

> It doesn't cause another block (Aching Beauty would not be triggered, for
> example); it just trumps Form of Mist, and prevents the action from continuing
> successfully.

My understanding of this is that Form of Mist has fizzled completely.
The original blocker is still a blocker - there is no new block.

>> Another thing. After Form of Mist ends the combat, it's the acting
>> player who has first dibs on playing the next card. Suppose he plays
>> another action modifier such as Command of the Beast. Does this stop
>> the other guy from playing Psyche! because the game is no longer at
>> the end of a combat?
>
>Can't skip timing steps.

My question was sparked by the Psyche!/Fast Reactions clash in which a
player is deprived of an opportunity to act. That's the general issue
here - that someone can play a card which then stops the play of a
subsequent card.

As for "timing steps", this is not a term used by the rulebook and so
I'm not sure what you mean by it. But thinking about what the rules
actually say leads to another solution of the Psyche/Mist puzzle.

The general rule for VTES is that you execute cards as they are
played, right? This is a reasonable default - you just play the card
and do what it says right away. So, when you play Form of Mist, you
resolve the Combat Ends effect and the rulebook tells us that combat
ends "immediately". Because this has resolved, the opponent can't now
play Psyche! because that is a Combat card and they can only be played
during combat (1.6.3.4). For Psyche! to be useable after Form of
Mist, it would have to be a Reaction card - something that is played
in response to an action (the action which Form of Mist continues).

So, when can you play Psyche!? Obviously, it gets played during the
Press step, a combat step which the rulebook does describe. During
this step the players keep toggling the state of combat ending and
they are explicitly allowed to keep playing cards back and forth until
they both pass. Psyche! is played when one might otherwise play a
press to continue. It's inferior form is a press and its superior
form is a correspondingly superior type of press, because it cannot be
countered by another press.

I think the mistake has arisen because Psyche has been treated as a
reaction or interrupt card - something that is played in response to
the instantaneous event of combat ending. It isn't; it's a type of
Press and can only be played during that step.

Note, by contrast, that Fast Reactions _is_ a Reaction card and its
timing and template are quite consistent with the rules. When I look
at these cards, I immediately notice the difference because I use
nothing but VTES cards and the card type is glaringly obvious - Combat
cards are red while Reaction cards are blue. This wasn't the case
originally.

The misreading of Psyche! has been exacerbated because S:CE cards like
Majesty are so prevalent and frustrating that many players have
welcomed any possibility of countering them. But the designers
clearly wanted "Combat Ends" to mean exactly that - that's why it
beats First Strike, as discussed elsewhere. This is not meant to be a
beat-em-up game like Rage and that's why it's so easy to shut down
combat.

Andrew

Messages.Author: Matt
Messages.Body:
It seems pretty obvious why superior psyche! dos not have to played
only in the press step. The card text at superior is pretty specific.

"
Only usable at the end of a combat when both combatants are still

ready. Enter combat with the opposing minion. This is a new combat.
"

By card text, it is specifically designed to be used after combat has
ended. Thus it ignores the normal limitation on when combat cards can
be played.

In case that was in doubt, the various ruling on the card support that
fact, just in case people argued "it's just a combat card."

http://whitestar.ddg.com/vtes/monger/showcard.html?ID=615

Seems pretty simple.

Wisefool

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On Wed, 30 Jan 2002 08:23:03 -0500, LSJ wrote:

>> The general rule for VTES is that you execute cards as they are
>> played, right?
>

>Yes.

I now realise that this is not the case with Form of Mist. Because
it's a strike, it is played in one phase and resolved in another. So,
while the rulebook says that "this effect ends combat immediately",
this doesn't happen when the card is played. This makes the situation
more like the Press step in that you have a state where combat is
"about to end", as Telepathic Tracking puts it. Psyche! should be
played at this point which stops it being an exception to the rule
that combat cards are played during combat. It also explains why it
trumps Form of Mist - because it is resolved before it, even though it
is played afterwards.

A general difficulty I have with this stuff is that there are hidden
phases in the sequence of play which are not obvious from the
rulebook. The classic case is the pre-manuever step in combat. These
derive their existence from card text not the rules (other than the
Golden Rule) and so it's difficult to be aware of them without knowing
all the cards in the game (and I don't). This leads to misplays when
the non-phasing player wants to play such a card when the other player
has already moved on to the next rulebook phase. Magic has formal
rules for backing up in this situation, I believe, but I'm not sure
what the strict situation is in VTES. The LA players (who I may face
at Orccon) are tough about backing-up and so the matter may arise.

>Yeah, then you had to "guess" based only on the icon. Pah.

It appears that there was a general reversal in 1998 which was based
on this point that combat cards can only be played during combat.
There must therefore have been some confusion about this before.

Andrew
